content: Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (ISD) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that manifests as redness and greasy scaling rashes in infants and young children. When it occurs on the scalp, it is commonly referred to as cradle cap. Although the condition is benign and self-limiting, it can cause significant concern for parents. ISD typically resolves within weeks to months, though in rare cases, it may persist for years. The effectiveness of commonly recommended treatments for ISD remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of various interventions for ISD in children from birth to 24 months of age. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared any treatment for ISD to no treatment, placebo, or other treatments. The primary outcomes assessed were changes in the severity of the condition and the percentage of infants experiencing adverse effects or intolerance to treatment. A secondary outcome was the improvement in quality of life (QoL) as reported by parents. The review included six RCTs involving 310 children, with outcomes reported for 297 participants. Most of the children were under seven months old, and only two participants were older than one year. The severity of ISD was described as mild to moderate in two studies, while other studies either did not specify baseline severity or described it in terms of body surface area affected. The studies were conducted in various countries, including Thailand, Israel, the USA, France, and Australia, and were likely carried out in pediatric outpatient clinics. Two studies compared oral biotin (a B-group vitamin) to placebo. One study did not report changes in severity but instead measured the duration of the rash, while the other study reported no statistically significant difference between biotin and placebo but did not provide raw data. Neither study reported adverse events. Two studies compared proprietary products to placebo. One trial evaluated a non-steroidal cream (Promiseb) and found a 96% success rate compared to 92% with placebo, with no adverse events reported. Another trial assessed a combination of lactamide MEA gel (a moisturizing agent) and shampoo, which showed better results (81.4% reduction in lesional score) compared to shampoo alone (70.2%; P = 0.0092). No adverse events were reported, and signs of discomfort were similar between groups. Two studies compared topical corticosteroids to other products. In one trial, hydrocortisone 1% lotion was compared to licochalcone 0.025% lotion. Both treatments showed similar cure rates (95.8% for hydrocortisone versus 97.1% for licochalcone), with one participant in the licochalcone group developing increased erythema. No other adverse events were reported. In another trial, flumethasone pivalate 0.02% ointment was compared to eosin 2% aqueous solution. Both treatments resulted in a reduction in body surface area affected by the rash, with less than 10% involvement in all infants by day 10. No adverse events were reported. None of the included studies measured quality of life (QoL) outcomes. Additionally, no trials were identified that tested commonly used treatments such as mineral oils, salicylic acid, or antifungal agents. The evidence from this review is of very low certainty, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness and safety of the studied treatments. Most studies had unclear risks of bias, with some showing high risks of performance, attrition, and detection bias. The evidence was further limited by small sample sizes, low event rates, indirectness of outcomes, and poor reporting of trial details. Despite the generally favorable prognosis of ISD regardless of treatment, the lack of high-quality evidence limits the interpretation of these findings. Future research should focus on conducting large, well-designed, and well-reported trials to evaluate commonly recommended treatments, such as emollients, shampoos, antifungals, and steroids. These studies should include standardized and validated outcome measures, such as adverse events, severity scores, and QoL assessments. Trials should also be conducted in primary care settings, where most cases of ISD are managed, and should compare interventions to placebo, no treatment, or standard care.
